title: Milestone: Thinking in Chances
objective: After this level you can connect percentages, averages, chance, expected value and base rates to judge one real-world risk.
summary: One scary headline, taken apart with the first half of the tree: percents, averages, chance, expected value and base rates, all together.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to take apart one scary headline.
cards.body: Here it is, made up but typical: "Late-night snacking doubles your risk of a rare condition, and a new test can spot it!" Everything you need to judge it, you already have.

cards.headline: Four questions for any risk
cards.body: One: doubled from what? Ask for the absolute risks before and after, and over how long. Two: per what? A risk is a rate, so check what it is counted out of. Three: how common is it to begin with? Start from the base rate. Four: if a test says yes, how many yeses are real? For a rare condition, many can be false alarms.

items.label: The headline says
points: A new test can spot it

items.label: You ask
points: From 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000? That is 1 extra per 10,000
For a rare condition, how many positives are real?

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway, in chances
learned: Why a good test for a rare condition can give mostly false alarms, and how base rates explain it.
How to read a percent change, a rate or "doubles your risk" by first asking: out of what?
Which average fits lopsided numbers like income, and how spread shows what an average hides.
Why the casino wins in the long run, even though no streak ever makes a win "due".

questions.prompt: A risk rises from 2% to 3%. Which description is correct?

options.label: Up 1 percent, a 1 point relative rise
options.rationale: Mixed up: it is 1 point, and a 50% relative rise.

options.label: Up 50 percentage points
options.rationale: Subtract: 3 minus 2 is 1 point.

options.label: Up 1 percentage point, a 50% relative rise
Up 3 percentage points
options.rationale: 3% is where it ends, not how much it rose.

questions.explanation: Subtract for points (3 minus 2 = 1 point); divide by the start for the relative rise (1 ÷ 2 = 50%).

questions.prompt: Why do reports on typical household income usually quote the median, not the mean?

options.label: The mean is much harder to work out from census data
options.rationale: Both are easy to work out; the issue is what they describe.

options.label: A few very high incomes pull the mean above most households
The median always comes out higher, which looks better
options.rationale: For income the median is lower: $83,730 against $121,000 in 2024.

options.label: Only the median counts every household's income
options.rationale: It's the other way round: the mean counts every value.

questions.explanation: Income has a long tail of high earners that lifts the mean. The median, the middle household, stays put, so it shows what is typical.

questions.prompt: At Monte Carlo in 1913, black came up 26 times in a row. What was the chance of red on the next spin?

options.label: Much higher than usual, since red was overdue
options.rationale: The wheel keeps no score; nothing is ever due.

options.label: Much lower, since the wheel was on a black streak
options.rationale: A streak doesn't make black likelier either.

options.label: Impossible to say until the streak had ended
options.rationale: Each spin is independent, so the chance is known.

options.label: Exactly what it was on the very first spin

questions.explanation: Each spin is independent, so red's chance on spin 27 was the same as on spin 1. The crowd that thought red was due lost millions.

questions.prompt: Any roulette player can get lucky tonight. Why can the casino still count on keeping its edge?

options.label: Over many bets, results settle close to the expected value
The wheel is secretly tilted to favor the house
options.rationale: No tricks needed: the payouts are set as if there were 36 pockets.

options.label: Lucky players are banned before they can win much
options.rationale: The edge works without stopping anyone from winning.

options.label: Every player loses a little on every single spin
options.rationale: Single spins win or lose; only the long-run average is fixed.

questions.explanation: Each bet pays as if the wheel had 36 pockets, so its expected value is negative. Across thousands of bets, the law of large numbers keeps the casino's take close to that average: about 5.26 cents per dollar.

questions.prompt: A good test for a rare condition comes back positive. What should you ask before worrying?

options.label: Whether the test was expensive
options.rationale: Price says nothing about how many positives are real.

options.label: How common the condition is to begin with
Whether the result arrived quickly
options.rationale: Speed says nothing about how many positives are real.

options.label: How many tests the lab ran that day
options.rationale: The base rate matters, not the lab's workload.

questions.explanation: With a rare condition, false alarms from healthy people can outnumber true cases. The base rate tells you how many.

options.label: Trusting a statistic just because an expert presented it in court
options.rationale: That can be a problem, but the fallacy is a specific mix-up.

options.label: Refusing to allow any numbers at all as evidence in a courtroom
options.rationale: The fallacy is misreading a number, not avoiding numbers.

options.label: Treating how unlikely the evidence is by chance as the chance of innocence
Rounding a very small chance of the evidence down to zero
options.rationale: The error is about which chance is being described.

questions.explanation: A tiny chance of the evidence arising innocently is not the chance of innocence. Rival explanations must be compared.

questions.prompt: A headline says late-night snacking doubles your risk of a rare condition. What should you ask first?

options.label: How many people read the headline?
options.rationale: Readership doesn't change the risk.

options.label: Does the condition have a long name?
options.rationale: The name says nothing about the risk.

options.label: Was the study published this year?
options.rationale: Recent or not, you still need the numbers.

options.label: Doubled from what, and over how long?

questions.explanation: "Doubles" is a relative risk. Ask for the absolute risks before and after, over a set time.
